eradicate

/ih-RAD-ih-kayt/ - the stress falls on RAD · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Eradicate means to destroy or wipe out completely.

After the third infestation in two years, the landlord hired a crew with orders to eradicate the termites — every colony, every queen.

Example

Screwworm flies once cost American ranchers millions of animals a year. Starting in the 1950s, technicians raised billions of the flies, sterilized the males with radiation, and dropped them from airplanes week after week; wild females that mated with them left no offspring. Territory by territory the map went clean, and by 1966 the United States had eradicated the pest — not rare, gone.

Eradicate is the exact word for that campaign, because it means to destroy or wipe out completely — the goal is zero, not fewer. The word's own anatomy says so: e- plus radix, to pull out by the root, the gardener's one guarantee that a weed will not return. Reduce and control leave survivors; eradicate ends the line.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

eliminate: To eliminate is to get rid of something, with no promise about completeness — a team eliminated from one tournament is back the next year. To eradicate is to wipe out completely: zero left, anywhere, ever. Elimination clears a space; eradication ends the line.

exterminate: To exterminate is to kill off living things, usually pests, and the word stays close to actual killing. Eradicate reaches wider — you can eradicate a disease, an illegal practice, or a stubborn error, none of which die in the exterminator's sense — and it always promises zero.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep it alive and safe

protect: to shield it from harm

Where it sits · how completely the problem is stamped out

curb → contain → eradicate

curb vs. eradicate: Curb sits far below eradicate — the numbers stop climbing, but the problem lives on where it is, nothing like the zero eradicate demands.

contain vs. eradicate: Contain goes further than curb — the outbreak is penned inside a boundary — but eradicate claims the most: nothing left to pen, anywhere.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-: out (a form of ex-)

Root — radic: root (Latin radix)

Suffix — -ate: verb ending

Put it together: E- (out) + radic (root) + -ate = to tear out by the roots. Latin farmers coined eradicare for the weeding that actually works: take the root and the plant cannot come back. English keeps the promise — what is eradicated is gone at the source, with nothing left to regrow.

Use the root in a new word: radish: She sliced a peppery radish paper-thin over the salad and passed the bowl down the table.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / campaign language

Eradicate is the word for campaigns against living, spreading things — diseases, pests, stubborn practices — and it promises zero. Its unit-mates divide the labor: obliterate erases all trace of a thing, raze levels a structure to the ground, and pillage merely robs. If survivors remain, you have reduced or contained, not eradicated.
